newsitem.title: UK: BOE proposals seen as shot in arm for money market.
newsitem.headline: BOE proposals seen as shot in arm for money market.

text.p: Sterling money market and gilt repo dealers welcomed news on Wednesday that the Bank of England plans to include gilt repos in its daily money market operations from next year and to widen the group of partipants.
"This can only serve to broaden and deepen the gilt repo market...it's what we've been waiting for and should unleash another wave of players," said a repo trader at a UK bank.
The impact of more assets and players will have other knock-on effects on the domestic money market, traders said.
"It should help to reduce the volatility in overnight rates in the money market and generate a bit volume and liquidity," said one money broker.
UK market dealers are often hostage to wide swings in overnight rates if shortages linger in the money market. The inclusion of more eligible assets in daily operations should help alleviate this.
"It should certainly make the money markets more liquid," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.
"It has had to rely too heavily on the bill market over the years when there are only around 15 billion stg of them in the system, the majority of which are held by the clearing banks."

The Bank of England's unique method of providing liquidity to the UK money market involves buying bills at set rates from discount houses, which are "middlemen" between the central bank and UK clearing banks.

Bank of England executive director Ian Plenderleith said the proposals were designed to take account of the successful development of Britain's fledgling gilt repo market, which has grown steadily since its introduction in January 1996.
By August, it had reached 60 billion stg outstanding repos with daily turnover of 15 billion stg.

The Bank said the proposed changes, which follow consultation with British banks and brokers, were also consistent with the "direction and spirit of proposals under discussion at the European Monetary Institute" (EMI).

But Plenderleith stressed that bringing British money market operations into line with those being discussed by the EMI -- which is the forerunner of the European Central Bank -- "was not the main motive" behind the proposals.

Some UK traders and economists believe introducing gilt repos to the system would be an initial step towards more radical reform of the way the BOE operates in the UK money market, bringing it more into line with European counterparts.
But analysts said should the UK sign up to European economc and monetary union at the January 1999 launch date or afterwards, other key changes were a virtual certainty.

Most signficantly, the system of banks' balancing their accounts with the Bank of England on a daily basis would probably have to change to a minimum reserve system averaged over a month or so, they said.

Under the new proposals, London's seven discount houses will lose their exclusive right to deal directly with the Bank of England. However, officials and bankers said their business need not be damaged by the long-awaited changes.
Cater Allen chairman James Barclay said in a statement that his firm should benefit from the move.

"Our money market subsidiary Cater Allen Limited already holds a leading position in the gilt repo market. We believe we will benefit from the introduction of the Bank as a major daily user," he said.
Most dealers said they expected the banks, securities firms and building societies who actively participate in the Bank's twice-monthly repo facility to take part in daily operations.

"The fortnightly repo has been open to these other counterparties for around three years, and they are likely to be the first dealers to participate in the new daily repo," said one trader. This facility will cease when the new operations are introduced.

The Bank of England also plans to change the timing of its afternoon operations to 1440 GMT instead of 1400 GMT. It hopes this will enable most players to cover any shortage earlier than at present and not be forced to hang on for late assistance.
Under the present system the Bank has the option of providing assistance at set times, starting with around 0945 GMT, then 1200 GMT, 1400 GMT and finally late help at 1445 GMT.
Under the new regulation, the bank will also limit any late assistance to clearing banks and charge them a flat rate of 1/4 percent above the repo rate.

Currently, unspecified late assistance is offered at two levels, one tranche at official interest rates -- which are now six percent -- and the other 1/4 percentage point above official rates. Normal assistance is provided at just below official interest rates.
